Throughout, $c>0$ and $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is the oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], with displacement space
$V$; $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and $x:I\to A$ is a $C^1$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function
$\tau:I\to J$ and inverse $\rho:J\to I$
([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]). By that
lemma $\tau$ is $C^1$ with

$$\tau'(s)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0 \qquad (s\in I),$$

$\tau$ is strictly increasing, $J=\tau[I]$ is an interval with at least two
elements, and $\rho:J\to I$ is $C^1$ with $\rho'(\tau(s))=1/\tau'(s)>0$ for
every $s\in I$.

**(a) The proper-time derivative.** Let $P:I\to V$ be a $C^1$ map, its
derivative $P'$ being the derivative of a $V$-valued function of one real
variable, read componentwise in any ordered basis of $V$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The **proper-time
derivative of $P$** is the map $\dot P:I\to V$ defined by

$$\dot P(s):=\frac{P'(s)}{\tau'(s)} .$$

This is well defined because $\tau'(s)>0$ for every $s\in I$, so the scalar
division by $\tau'(s)$ is a legitimate vector-space operation on $V$. The
definition does not depend on the basis of $V$ in which $P'$ is read: a change
of basis acts on the coordinates of $P'(s)$, and hence on those of
$\dot P(s)$, by the same constant invertible linear map, which commutes with
multiplication by the scalar $1/\tau'(s)$. Since $P'$ and $1/\tau'$ are
continuous, $\dot P$ is continuous; equivalently, the proper-time derivative of
a $C^1$ field is a continuous field.

**The proper-time reading.** Since $\tau$ is a strictly increasing bijection
$I\to J$ with inverse $\rho$, one has $\rho(\tau(s))=s$ and therefore
$(P\circ\rho)\circ\tau=P$ on $I$. Fix $s\in I$; the components of $P$ in a
basis of $V$ are differentiable at $s$ and $\rho$ is differentiable at
$\tau(s)$, so the scalar chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule]]) applied to each
component of $P\circ\rho$ gives

$$P'(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s))\,\tau'(s), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \dot P(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s)) .$$

At an endpoint of $I$ this is the one-sided reading of the derivative, as in
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. Thus $\dot P$ is exactly the
derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter of the field $P$ read
along the parametrisation $s\mapsto\tau(s)$; for every $u\in J$ the chain rule
on $J$ gives $(P\circ\rho)'(u)=P'(\rho(u))\rho'(u)=\dot P(\rho(u))$.

**(b) The four-force notation.** Let $m>0$ be constant and suppose the
four-velocity $U:I\to V$ of $x$ is $C^1$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]); by that definition $U$ is
always continuous, and $U$ is $C^1$ whenever the worldline $x$ is $C^2$. Then
$P:=mU$ is a $C^1$ map $I\to V$ and $F:=\dot P$ is called the **four-force**
on the particle. In an inertial frame the components of $F$ are the
derivatives of the components of the four-momentum with respect to the
proper-time parameter: writing $P^a(u)$ for the components of $P$ as a
function of the proper-time parameter $u=\tau(s)$, one has
$F^a(s)=\frac{d}{du}P^a(u)\big|_{u=\tau(s)}$.

**(c) Scope.** This item introduces a derivative and a name only. It asserts no
force law, no field equation, no equation of motion and no existence or
uniqueness of solutions of any equation of motion; in particular the
hypothesis that $U$ be $C^1$ is a regularity hypothesis on the given
worldline, not a dynamical statement. The identities satisfied by $F$ for a
stipulated four-momentum field are proved in
[[lem-sr-four-force-and-work-energy-identities]], and a physical force law
requires the separate model premise [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]].
The names four-momentum and four-force, and the units in which the components
of $P$ and $F$ are measured, belong to the framework's coordinate and unit
conventions ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]); the
mathematical content asserted here is the derivative construction (a) and the
notation (b) alone. No choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline with
proper-time function $\tau$ and inverse $\rho$ of
[[def-sr-proper-time]] and [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]].

**(a) Four-velocity.** The **four-velocity** of $x$ is the map $U : I \to V$
defined by

$$U(s) := \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $U(s)$ is the tangent at parameter value $s$ of the proper-time
parametrized worldline $x \circ \rho$, read at the proper-time parameter
$\tau(s)$: by clause (iv) of [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]],
$(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = U(s)$. The map $U$ is continuous,
$U(s)$ is future timelike for every $s \in I$, and $U$ does not depend on the
base point chosen for $\tau$ (changing the base point adds a constant to
$\tau$).

**(b) Four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$, that is, $x'$ is differentiable
with continuous derivative ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), the
**four-acceleration** of $x$ is the map $A : I \to V$ defined by

$$A(s) := \frac{U'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,U'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $A(s)$ is the derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter
of the four-velocity along the worldline: by the chain rule,
$A(s) = (U \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$. The map $A$ is continuous.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

**(d) Names and scope.** The names four-velocity and four-acceleration are the
model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function
$\tau(s) = c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(u),x'(u))}\,du$ for a base point
$s_0 \in I$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]]). Then:

**(i)** $\tau$ is differentiable at every $s \in I$, with one-sided derivatives
at the endpoints of $I$, and

$$\tau'(s) = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr)} > 0$$

for every $s \in I$; since $\tau'$ is this composition of continuous maps,
$\tau$ is $C^{1}$ on $I$.

**(ii)** $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$, hence injective, and its image
$J := \tau[I]$ is an order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with at least two
elements, so $\tau : I \to J$ is a bijection.

**(iii)** The inverse $\rho : J \to I$ of $\tau$ is continuous and strictly
increasing, and it is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of $J$ with

$$\rho'\bigl(\tau(s)\bigr) = \frac{1}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} > 0 ;$$

hence $\rho$ is $C^{1}$ on $J$.

**(iv)** The reparametrized curve $y := x \circ \rho : J \to A$ is a $C^{1}$
future timelike worldline whose tangent at the proper-time parameter $\tau(s)$ is

$$(x \circ \rho)'\bigl(\tau(s)\bigr) = \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

in particular $y$ is parametrized by its own proper time up to the additive
constant of the base point.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes the domains of $\delta$ and $\times$.
The Lorentz form, the fixed orientation of $V$, and the time orientation $C^+$
are data of the model independent of the named inertial frame
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). The Euclidean spatial structure instead
requires the choice of a time axis $e_0$; it is not an additional
frame-independent structure on the whole of $V$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), $c>0$, and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with stationary observer $n:=e_0$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); let $E_n,q_n$ be the observer
quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]].

**(a)** For every $P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ the coordinate components of $P$ in
the frame are $(P^0,P^1,P^2,P^3)=(E_n(P)/c,\,q^1,q^2,q^3)$, where
$q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3q^ie_i$; if $P$ is future timelike then
$E^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2\sum_{i=1}^3(q^i)^2$ with $E=E_n(P)$.

**(b)** Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) whose chart coordinate path is
$t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w:=r'$ and
$\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]],
[[def-rational-power]]); then $|w|<c$, the four-velocity is
$U=\gamma_w(c,w)$ by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(e),
and for $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant the components are $P=m\gamma_w(c,w)$, that
is $E_n(P)=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3m\gamma_ww^ie_i$.

$n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(n,v)=0\}$ for the rest space of $n$,
$h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ for the rest
projection and $|w|:=\sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ for the norm on $n^\perp$
([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c)); recall from that

$$E_n(P):=-c\,\eta(P,n), \qquad q_n(P):=h(P),$$

and, when $P$ is nonzero future causal, define the **invariant mass** of $P$ by

$$m(P):=\frac{\sqrt{-\eta(P,P)}}{c} .$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.
If $a>0$ and $r\in\mathbb Q$, then the real power $a^r=\exp(r\log a)$ agrees with the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. For $r>0$, both conventions also give $0^r=0$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.
